performers: William McColl, basset clarinet; University of Washington Symphony Orchestra, Abraham Kaplan
question: What tells you that the refrain has returned: its rhythm, its melodic shape, or the recovery of A major?
intro: The finale begins with the soloist rather than a long orchestral introduction. Its recurring refrain gives the listener a point of recognition while the episodes explore darker harmony and different relationships between clarinet and orchestra.

sections.label: Refrain · the soloist leads
sections.mNote: A major and a buoyant compound metre

cues.title: The soloist starts the dance
cues.text: The clarinet opens the finale with a buoyant refrain above a light string accompaniment. Its compound metre groups the quick notes into larger rocking beats; try hearing the dance in those larger units.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, III, PDF p. 36, Rondo, Allegro, 6/8; report begins with an A-major profile and comparatively low relative level. The opening scoring is read from the score.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keep the refrain in mind
cues.text: Notice the refrain’s mixture of short repeated notes and longer curves. Remembering its shape will help you recognise it after the intervening episodes, even when the surrounding orchestration changes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, opening refrain, PDF pp. 36–38; report 0:25–0:45 retains the opening tonal profile. This is a general listening task, not a claimed new entry.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The concerto’s first listener
cues.text: Anton Stadler is the player for whom Mozart writes the concerto. His extended-range clarinet helps explain why the solo line can make such a large part of its expressive life in the lower register.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, “Swan Song: Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto”, https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.

cues.title: An episode opens out
cues.text: The first contrasting episode gives the clarinet a new line to develop. The refrain’s easy recognition gives way to a more exploratory continuation, with the dominant region becoming important.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, first episode, PDF pp. 39–42; report has a quieter span from 1:25, then a boundary at 1:50 and an E-centred profile through much of 2:00–2:30. Section marker 1:24 is provisional.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The line stretches further
cues.text: The solo writing moves through longer runs and changes of register. Listen for how the supporting strings keep the metre legible while the clarinet’s line seems to range beyond the simple proportions of the refrain.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, first episode continuation, PDF pp. 41–43; report boundaries 2:26 and 2:36 precede a lower-level, less stable passage. No specific low-register reconstruction is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recognition before another departure
cues.text: The refrain’s familiar shape returns briefly. It acts as a point of orientation rather than a final destination: the orchestra will again lead the movement away from this easy A-major manner.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, refrain return and ensuing tutti, PDF pp. 43–44; report returns to an A-major profile around 2:50–3:10 after the quieter 2:40 window.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dance enters the minor
cues.text: The central passage turns towards F♯ minor. The solo clarinet remains agile, but the harmony changes the character of its motion; the same compound metre can carry uncertainty as well as ease.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, central episode, PDF pp. 44–47; report boundary 3:28 and sustained F♯-minor estimates at 3:30–3:45 corroborate the score-derived region.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: More than three movements
cues.text: The concerto’s surviving printed tradition is not the whole story of its sound. Its complete autograph is lost, and editions for the ordinary clarinet alter notes that lie below that instrument’s range.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, “Swan Song: Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto”, https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.

cues.title: An earlier contrast returns
cues.text: The movement revisits contrasting solo material before giving the opening refrain its full final return. Listen for recognition at a smaller scale: an episode can come back even when the main refrain has not yet settled the form.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, later solo material, PDF pp. 47–50; report moves from D-centred windows at 4:15–4:30 towards A around 4:35–4:45. The marker at 4:32 is a broad formal estimate; internal brief refrain fragments are not separately timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A darker interruption
cues.text: The later episode does not remain entirely in a bright major mode. Chromatic turns and more exposed moments interrupt the easy movement, making the eventual return of the refrain something to hear rather than merely predict.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, later episode and pauses, PDF pp. 48–50; report boundaries 4:52, 4:58, 5:02 and 5:14 lead into A-minor-centred windows at 5:15–5:25.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Let the pause have weight
cues.text: In this part of the movement, reduced sound and suspended motion matter as much as the runs. Listen for how the music resumes its forward movement after a more hesitant span.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, fermatas in the later episode, PDF p. 49; report low-level windows at 5:30 and 5:35, followed by strongest boundary 5:38 and renewed onset activity. The cue does not identify a particular improvised note.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The refrain comes home
cues.text: The full refrain restores the opening’s A-major character. Compare the return with your memory of the first phrase: recognition now carries the weight of the intervening minor-mode and chromatic passages.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, return into the final refrain, PDF pp. 51–52; report boundary 6:16 and stable A-major profile from 6:15–6:35. The return marker at 6:12 is provisional.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A self-built basset clarinet
cues.text: William McColl performs here on a basset clarinet of his own construction. The University of Washington orchestra and Abraham Kaplan join him in December 1987; the documentation does not identify a particular performing edition.
cues.evidence: Wikimedia Commons file description and Soni Ventorum archive, Mozart K. 622, https://soniventorum.com/soniventorum_archives.html.

cues.title: Soloist and ensemble share momentum
cues.text: Listen for the movement passing between the clarinet and the orchestra instead of belonging permanently to one of them. The solo flourishes are part of the closing argument, not a detached display outside it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, final refrain continuation, PDF pp. 52–57; report strong 7:25–7:30 windows are followed by more moderate relative level across 7:35–7:55. No exact handover is asserted.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The ending stays mobile
cues.text: The later solo writing keeps the quick figures alive as the music prepares its last cadence. Follow the bass beneath the decoration: the closing goal grows clearer while the surface remains active.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, closing solo and orchestral paragraphs, PDF pp. 56–58; report retains the A-major profile through 8:00–8:25, with a lower-level window at 8:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A major closes firmly
cues.text: The final orchestral statements bring the concerto to an A-major close. The ending gathers the movement’s energy into clear cadences rather than letting the dance dissolve into a fade.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf III, final page 58; report’s strongest late relative-level windows are 8:35–8:45, followed by the decay near the 8:51 endpoint.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A familiar close permits departure
transitions.how: The first refrain and its orchestral continuation establish A major. A lighter solo paragraph then opens a contrasting route towards the dominant, E. The new material grows out of the same 6/8 movement, so a change of melodic character does not need a change of tempo.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf III, PDF pp. 38–41; report falls from a stronger 1:15–1:20 span to a quieter 1:25–1:45 passage, before the clearer E-region boundary at 1:50.

transitions.title: The dance finds its tonic
transitions.how: The episode’s more extended solo writing contracts towards a return to A major. The familiar refrain provides the recognition point, and the orchestra reinforces it. Its brevity makes this a hinge into further exploration rather than the final close.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf III, PDF pp. 42–44; report lower-level 2:40 window followed by the return of the A-major profile around 2:50–3:10.

transitions.title: The orchestra redirects the dance
transitions.how: A full orchestral passage carries the movement away from the refrain and into F♯ minor. The clarinet resumes against a lighter accompaniment. The contrast is harmonic and textural: the compound metre continues, but the relative minor changes the line’s expressive surroundings.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf III, PDF pp. 44–46; report strong 3:05–3:20 windows, followed by boundary 3:28 and quieter F♯-minor region.

transitions.title: Development becomes recollection
transitions.how: The central exploration works through changing keys and fragments before earlier solo material becomes recognisable again. The texture remains conversational rather than turning into a ceremonial return. This is a broad recapitulatory passage; its brief internal references to the refrain are not separately mapped.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf III, PDF pp. 47–50; report D-major region at 4:15–4:30, A-centred passage around 4:35–4:45, then renewed contrasting boundaries. Formal marker 4:32 is approximate.

transitions.title: Hesitation gives way to recognition
transitions.how: The later episode includes chromatic turns and pauses before the refrain re-establishes A major. The solo line recovers the opening’s recognisable rhythmic shape, and the orchestra enlarges the return. The remaining music extends this home-key close rather than opening another large episode.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf III, PDF pp. 49–52; report low-level span at 5:30–5:35, renewed motion at 5:38, and A-major profile from 6:15 with boundary 6:16. The marker is provisional.

source.title: Mozart, Clarinet Concerto K. 622, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke XII/20 (1881), plate W.A.M. 622; shared orchestral fabric only

The first refrain’s orchestral continuation includes flutes, bassoons and horns.

A fuller orchestral passage follows the brief refrain return.
The central minor-mode episode is led by the solo clarinet.
Later solo passages exchange material with the strings; wind interjections are intermittent.
The final refrain restores the solo-led opening character.
The later refrain alternates orchestral statements with continuing solo passagework.

composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781
Italian opera seria and opera buffa; German Singspiel with spoken dialogue
K. or KV = Ludwig von Köchel’s catalogue, first published in 1862 and repeatedly revised
composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
